exercises.prompt: Kofi carefully snaps a bar magnet in half, right through the middle. What does he end up with?

options.label: Two magnets, each with its own north and south pole
options.feedback: Yes. Every piece of a magnet, however small, has both poles. A north pole on its own has never been found.

options.label: A north pole on one piece and a south pole on the other
options.feedback: Not yet. That is what you might expect, but magnetic poles always come in pairs: each piece gets a new pole at the break.

options.label: Two pieces of iron that are no longer magnetic
options.feedback: Not yet. Breaking a magnet doesn't remove its magnetism. Each half is still a magnet.

hints: This is where magnets are different from electric charges.
Can you ever have a north pole on its own?
exercises.solution: He gets **two smaller magnets, each with a north and a south pole**. Magnetic poles always come in pairs: a new south pole appears on the half that kept the old north pole, and a new north pole on the other half. Cut them again and the same happens. This is a real difference from electric charge, where a positive or negative charge can exist on its own.

exercises.prompt: In 1820 Hans Christian Ørsted saw a compass needle swing when he switched on a current in a nearby wire. What did this show?

options.label: An electric current makes a magnetic field.
options.feedback: Yes. The current's magnetic field pushed on the compass needle, which is a small magnet.

options.label: A magnet makes an electric current.
options.feedback: Not yet. That is the reverse effect, discovered by Faraday in 1831, and it needs a *moving* magnet.

options.label: The wire was made of iron.
options.feedback: Not yet. The needle only moved when the current was on, so it was the current, not the material, that mattered.

options.label: Compasses don't work indoors.
options.feedback: Not yet. The compass worked perfectly: it was responding to a new magnetic field, the one made by the current.

hints: The needle moved only when the current was switched on.
exercises.solution: It showed that **an electric current makes a magnetic field**. A compass needle is a small magnet, and it only turns when a magnetic field pushes on it; since it moved only while the current flowed, the current itself must make a field. The field lines circle round the wire. This was the first link between electricity and magnetism, and it leads directly to electromagnets and motors.

exercises.prompt: Which of these would make an electromagnet **stronger**? Choose all that apply.

options.label: Winding more turns of wire on the coil
options.feedback: Yes. The fields of all the turns add together.

options.label: Putting an iron core inside the coil
options.feedback: Yes. Iron concentrates the field and makes it far stronger.

options.label: Increasing the current, safely
options.feedback: Yes. More current means a stronger field, as long as the wire and the battery don't overheat.

options.label: Replacing the iron core with a wooden one
options.feedback: Not yet. Wood isn't magnetic, so it would be like having no core at all: the magnet gets weaker.

options.label: Switching the current off
options.feedback: Not yet. An electromagnet needs current: switch it off and its magnetism disappears. That is what makes electromagnets so useful.

hints: Three things make an electromagnet stronger.
Think about the coil, the current and the core.
exercises.solution: **More turns, an iron core, and more current** all make an electromagnet stronger. The turns' fields add up; iron concentrates the field; and the field of each turn grows with the current. A wooden core does nothing, and switching off makes the magnetism disappear. (Raising the current also heats the wire, which is why real electromagnets are designed with wire thick enough for the current they carry.)

exercises.prompt: In a simple DC motor, what is the job of the split ring (the commutator)?

options.label: It reverses the current in the coil every half-turn, so the coil keeps turning the same way.
options.feedback: Yes. Without it, the pushes would reverse after half a turn and the coil would just rock back and forth.

options.label: It makes the magnets stronger.
options.feedback: Not yet. The split ring is part of the electrical connection to the coil; it doesn't affect the magnets.

options.label: It stores energy, like a small battery.
options.feedback: Not yet. The split ring is just two pieces of metal. It stores nothing; it switches connections.

options.label: It stops the motor from overheating.
options.feedback: Not yet. It has a different job: think about what would happen after the coil turned half-way if the current never changed direction.

hints: Imagine the coil has turned half-way. Which side is now where the other side used to be?
If the current kept the same direction, which way would the pushes now turn the coil?
exercises.solution: The split ring **reverses the current in the coil every half-turn**. After half a turn, each side of the coil has swapped places; if the current kept flowing the same way, the pushes would now turn the coil backwards, and it would rock to and fro and stop. The brushes slide from one half of the ring to the other at just the right moment, swapping the coil's connections to the battery, so the pushes always turn the coil the same way.

exercises.prompt: Mei pushes a magnet into a coil connected to a sensitive meter, and the needle flicks. Then she holds the magnet **still** inside the coil. What does the meter show?

options.label: Zero: no current flows while the magnet is still.
options.feedback: Yes. Induction needs a *changing* magnetic field. A magnet at rest makes no current.

options.label: A steady current, as long as the magnet stays in the coil.
options.feedback: Not yet. This is exactly what Faraday expected at first, and it is not what happens. Only change makes a current.

options.label: A larger current than while it was moving.
options.feedback: Not yet. Moving the magnet is what made the current. When it stops, the current stops.

hints: Faraday's discovery was subtle: what does induction need?
Is the magnetic field through the coil changing while the magnet rests inside it?
exercises.solution: The meter shows **zero**. Electromagnetic induction makes a voltage only while the magnetic field through the coil is *changing*. While Mei pushes the magnet in, the field through the coil grows and a current flows; once the magnet is still, the field stops changing and the current stops. Pulling it out would make the needle flick the other way.

exercises.prompt: A generator with one north and one south pole makes one complete wave of alternating voltage for each turn. In a country whose grid runs at **60 Hz** (60 waves per second), how many **revolutions per minute** (rpm) must such a generator turn?

feedback.message: Close: 60 is the number of turns per **second**. The question asks for turns per **minute**.
Not yet: 3000 rpm gives 50 Hz, the frequency in most of the world. This grid runs at 60 Hz.

hints: One turn makes one wave, so 60 waves per second needs 60 turns per second.
How many seconds are there in a minute?
exercises.solution: One turn makes one complete wave, so 60 Hz needs **60 turns every second**. A minute has 60 seconds, so that is $60 \times 60 = 3600$ turns per minute: **3600 rpm**. In a 50 Hz country the same kind of generator turns at $50 \times 60 = 3000$ rpm.

exercises.prompt: A small generator's peak voltage is proportional to its speed. At **500 rpm** it gives a peak of **4 V**. What peak voltage, in volts, does it give at **1500 rpm**?

feedback.message: Not yet: 8 V would be the voltage at 1000 rpm (twice the speed). 1500 rpm is three times 500 rpm.

hints: Proportional means: multiply the speed by some number, and the voltage is multiplied by the same number.
exercises.solution: The speed goes up by a factor of $1500 \div 500 = 3$. Because the voltage is proportional to the speed, it goes up by the same factor: $4 \times 3 =$ **12 V**. This is the straight-line pattern in the lesson's toy-generator table, where doubling the speed doubled the voltage.

exercises.prompt: Which of these sources makes electricity **without** spinning a generator?

options.label: A wind turbine
options.feedback: Not yet. The wind turns the blades, which turn a generator.

options.label: A hydroelectric dam
options.feedback: Not yet. Falling water spins turbines, which turn generators.

options.label: A nuclear power station
options.feedback: Not yet. Nuclear heat boils water into steam, which spins a turbine and a generator, just like a coal or gas station.

options.label: A solar panel
options.feedback: Yes. A solar cell turns light directly into electricity in a semiconductor, with no moving parts.

hints: Most power stations differ only in *what* spins the generator.
Which one has no moving parts at all?
exercises.solution: **Solar panels** are the exception. Wind, falling water and steam (from nuclear, coal, gas or geothermal heat) all spin turbines connected to generators, which use Faraday's induction. A solar cell turns light straight into electricity in a semiconductor, with no magnets and no moving parts, and gives direct current.
